```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  render = function(x, ...) {
    if (inherits(x, "shiny.appobj")) invisible() else knitr::knit_print(x, ...)
  }
)
```

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(blockr.core)
library(blockr.dock)
library(blockr.graph)
```

An app script for blockr.core 0.1 draws the DAG of its board with blockr.dag.
It passes the DAG's extension, which `new_dag_extension()` makes, to the `new_dock_board()` of blockr.dock 0.2.0.
Version 0.2 of blockr.core moves the board from R to the browser, as its migration notes describe (`vignette("migration-notes", package = "blockr.core")`).
On that version, blockr.graph draws the DAG, as a plugin that `new_graph_plugin()` makes.
The package blockr.dag stays with blockr.core 0.1.

These notes list each change that an app script needs to draw the DAG with blockr.graph 0.2.0 in place of blockr.dag.
They are written so that an AI can apply them to a script.
Each section names what a script calls in blockr.dag, says what takes its place, and shows the code of both.
A script follows the migration notes of blockr.core and blockr.dock too, since it builds its board with blockr.core, and the dock draws it (`vignette("migration-notes", package = "blockr.dock")`).

A script attaches blockr.graph in place of blockr.dag, as `library(blockr.graph)`.
The package blockr.dag imports functions that blockr.dock 0.2.1 no longer has, so a script that still attaches it stops at `library(blockr.dag)`.
No function of blockr.dag has an alias in blockr.graph ([The functions that go](#the-functions-that-go)).
So a script that calls a function with its package, as `blockr.dag::new_dag_extension()`, calls the function that takes its place, as `blockr.graph::new_graph_plugin()`.

## Boards that blockr.dag saved

A board that blockr.dock 0.2.0 saved with the DAG's extension opens on blockr.core 0.2 once blockr.convert has turned its file into a JSON board.
The migration notes of blockr.core and blockr.dock describe that conversion.
The conversion makes the DAG's plugin from the extension's state, with `new_graph_plugin()`:

- Each block keeps the position that the file holds for it.
- The layout keeps its direction and spacing, and its other settings take their defaults ([The layout](#the-layout)).
- No stack is collapsed, since the file does not record which stacks the DAG showed collapsed.

The file holds no position for a stack.
So as the board opens, the DAG places each stack that holds no block.
The DAG also drops the position of each block that the board lacks, such as a block that the conversion leaves out.
It raises a warning that names the block.

Until 14 August 2026, blockr.dock wrote an empty state for each extension.
So a file of blockr.dock 0.1.2 holds no state of the DAG, and the DAG lays such a board out as it opens.

## The DAG's plugin

In blockr.dag, `new_dag_extension()` makes the DAG's extension, which a script passes to `new_dock_board()` in `extensions`.
In blockr.graph, `new_graph_plugin()` makes the DAG's plugin, which a script passes to the `new_board()` of blockr.core in `plugins`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# blockr.dag
serve(
  new_dock_board(
    blocks = c(a = new_dataset_block("iris"), b = new_head_block()),
    links = new_link("a", "b"),
    extensions = new_dag_extension(
      positions = list(
        a = list(x = 200, y = 150),
        b = list(x = 200, y = 350)
      )
    )
  )
)
```

```{r}
# blockr.graph
serve(
  new_board(
    blocks = c(a = new_dataset_block("iris"), b = new_head_block()),
    links = new_link("a", "b"),
    plugins = list(
      new_graph_plugin(
        positions = list(
          a = list(x = 200, y = 150),
          b = list(x = 200, y = 350)
        )
      )
    )
  )
)
```

The function `new_graph_plugin(positions = list(), layout = graph_layout(), collapsed = character())` takes the DAG's state:

- Its `positions` are those that `new_dag_extension()` takes.
  Each gives where the node of a block sits on the canvas, by the block's id, as a list of the numbers `x` and `y`.
  The numbers count pixels of the canvas, with `x` to the right and `y` downwards.
  A position may also be a named vector, as `c(x = 200, y = 150)`.
- Its `layout` is what `graph_layout()` writes, in place of `dag_layout()` ([The layout](#the-layout)).
- Its `collapsed` is new.
  It holds the ids of the stacks that the DAG shows collapsed as the board opens, as `collapsed = "s1"`.
  In blockr.dag, every stack shows expanded as a board opens.

The function refuses `NULL` for `positions` and for `layout`, which `new_dag_extension()` takes for their defaults.
So a script that gives `positions = NULL` or `layout = NULL` drops the argument.
The function takes no `...` either.
In blockr.dag, `new_dag_extension()` passes its `...` on to the `new_dock_extension()` of blockr.dock.
A script drops each argument that it passes that way, since the argument would stop the call as an unused argument.

In blockr.dag, the DAG ignores the position of a block that the board lacks.
In blockr.graph, the DAG drops such a position as the board opens, and raises a warning that names the block.
So a script gives positions only for the blocks of its board.

Where a script gives no position at all, the DAG lays the whole board out as it opens, as blockr.dag does.
Where it gives positions for some blocks only, each of those blocks opens at its position.
The DAG places each of the other blocks after the blocks that the block reads from, at the nearest free spot.

Wherever blockr.graph is installed, `serve()` runs the DAG on every board by default, since its `plugins` default to every plugin class that `available_plugins()` lists.
A board without the DAG's plugin opens with the DAG's default state, which holds no position, so the DAG lays the board out.
The default of `serve()` may change, though, as the notes of blockr.core say.
So a script still puts the plugin on its board, and passes `new_graph_plugin()` where it passed `new_dag_extension()`, even without arguments:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# blockr.dag
serve(new_dock_board(extensions = new_dag_extension()))
```

```{r}
# blockr.graph
serve(new_board(plugins = list(new_graph_plugin())))
```

In blockr.dag, code in R sets the extension's `positions` and `layout` from outside, through an update of the board.
On blockr.core 0.2, nothing changes a board in R, as the notes of blockr.core say.
The DAG's commands change its state in the browser instead.
For example, the DAG's command `change_position` moves blocks, and its command `relayout` lays the board out again.

## The DAG's panel in the dock

In blockr.dag, `new_dock_board()` names the DAG's extension `dag`, after its class, unless the script names it in `extensions`.
A view or a grid of blockr.dock places the extension's panel by that name, with `ext("dag")` or by the panel id `"ext_panel-dag"`.
In blockr.graph, a plugin that the script leaves unnamed has no name.
So a script that places the DAG's panel names the plugin `dag` in the `plugins` of `new_board()`.
It places the panel with the `plg("dag")` of blockr.dock:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# blockr.dag
serve(
  new_dock_board(
    blocks = c(a = new_dataset_block("iris"), b = new_head_block()),
    links = new_link("a", "b"),
    extensions = new_dag_extension(),
    views = list(main = list(ext("dag"), blk("a"), blk("b"))),
    grids = list(main = dock_grid(ext("dag"), panels("a", "b")))
  )
)
```

```{r}
# blockr.graph
serve(
  new_board(
    blocks = c(a = new_dataset_block("iris"), b = new_head_block()),
    links = new_link("a", "b"),
    plugins = list(
      new_dock_plugin(
        views = list(
          main = dock_view(dock_grid(plg("dag"), panels("a", "b")))
        )
      ),
      dag = new_graph_plugin()
    )
  )
)
```

A script may give the DAG's extension another name in `extensions`, as `list(workflow = new_dag_extension())`.
It then gives the plugin the same name, as `list(workflow = new_graph_plugin())`.
A grid may also name the DAG's plugin by its class, `plg("graph_plugin", package = "blockr.graph")`, which needs no name.
Where a grid names a plugin that the board's `plugins` do not name, `new_board()` stops with an error that names the view and the plugin.

## The layout

In blockr.dag, `dag_layout()` writes the layout, which `new_dag_extension()` takes in `layout`.
In blockr.graph, `graph_layout()` writes it, and `new_graph_plugin()` takes it in `layout`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# blockr.dag
new_dag_extension(layout = dag_layout(direction = "LR", spacing = "compact"))
```

```{r}
# blockr.graph
new_graph_plugin(layout = graph_layout(direction = "LR", spacing = "compact"))
```

The function `graph_layout()` takes the `direction` and the `spacing` of `dag_layout()`, with the same values and defaults.
The direction is `"TB"`, from top to bottom, or `"LR"`, from left to right.
The spacing is `"normal"`, `"compact"` or `"loose"`.
The function also takes three settings that blockr.dag lacks:

- Its `placement` says how a block that a step adds gets its place.
  Under `"repulsion"`, the default, the block stays where the step puts it, and the DAG moves the blocks near it to make room.
  Under `"beside"`, the DAG moves the block to the nearest free spot, and moves no other block.
- Its `snap` says whether every position that the DAG sets snaps to a multiple of `snap_size`.
  It is `FALSE` by default.
- Its `snap_size` is the size that positions snap to, 20 pixels of the canvas by default.

The function `new_graph_plugin()` takes a layout that `graph_layout()` writes, and refuses any other.
In blockr.dag, `new_dag_extension()` also takes a list of the settings, as `list(direction = "LR")`.
A script wraps such a list in `graph_layout()`, as `graph_layout(direction = "LR")`.
The function `is_dag_layout()` goes, and a script tests `inherits(x, "graph_layout")` in its place.

In blockr.dag, G6 lays the whole board out again as blocks are added or removed, where the option `g6R.layout_on_data_change` is `TRUE`.
In blockr.graph, the DAG lays the whole board out again only when someone asks for it.
The user asks through the board action Layout, on the DAG's toolbar.
Layout runs the DAG's command `relayout`, which the assistant may run as well.
A block that a step adds gets its place from the layout's `placement`.

## Menus and the toolbar

In blockr.dag, the generic `context_menu_items()` gives the entries of the DAG's context menu, which `new_context_menu_entry()` makes.
The generic `toolbar_items()` gives the items of the DAG's toolbar, which `new_toolbar_item()` makes.
A package or a script adds an entry or an item through a method of either generic for the class `dag_extension`.

In blockr.graph, the DAG's menus are the menus of board actions of blockr.core.
A board action is what a user triggers from a menu, a button or a gesture.
It may ask the user for input, and then it runs commands, as one step that undo takes back.
A package offers what it adds to a menu as a board action, which one of its plugin classes lists in its module in JavaScript.
Core registers the board action with the class.
Every menu of the kinds of object that the board action names in its `on` then offers it, the DAG's menus among them.

So the generics go, with `new_context_menu_entry()`, `new_toolbar_item()`, `is_context_menu_entry()` and `is_toolbar_item()`, and nothing in R takes their place.
A script that defines a method of `context_menu_items()` or `toolbar_items()` moves what the method adds into a package, as a board action.
The notes of blockr.core say the same of a plugin that a script defines.
The package lists a plugin class in its `._BLOCKR_MODULES_`, as `?blockr.core::read_blocks_yml` describes.
The class's module, in JavaScript, lists the board actions in `boardActions`, each of the type `Omit<BoardAction, "package">` of `@blockr/core`.
A board action's definition gives its id alone.
Core registers the board action under the package of the plugin class that lists it.
This module offers the board action Lock block on every block.
The board action runs `change_block`, the command of blockr.core that changes a block.
Its `run` gets `core` as its third argument.
It names the command by the `Id` that `core.id()` gives:

```js
export const api = 1;

export default {
  boardActions: [
    {
      id: "lock_block_action",
      label: "Lock block",
      on: ["block"],
      category: "edit",
      run: (board, target, core) => [
        {
          id: core.id("blockr.core", "change_block"),
          args: { id: target.block, locked: true },
        },
      ],
    },
  ],
};
```

Each argument of an entry or an item of blockr.dag has this place in a board action:

| In blockr.dag | In a board action |
|---|---|
| The `name` of an entry, and the `tooltip` of an item | Its `label`, which a menu shows, and a button as its tooltip |
| The `id` of an entry or an item | Its `id` within the package, as `lock_block_action` |
| The `icon` of an item | Its `icon`, as SVG markup |
| The `condition` of an entry | Its `on`, the kinds of object whose menus offer it, and its `offers()`, which decides for each object |
| The `action` of an entry or an item, which changes the board in R | Its `run()`, which returns the commands that change the board, or its quick or advanced action, which asks the user first |
| The `js` of an entry or an item, which runs in the browser and sends an input to R | Nothing, since core runs the board action in the browser |
| The `retarget` of an entry, with which a pinned panel of the dock's sidebar follows the selection | Nothing, since a pinned place of an advanced action follows the selection, as the dock's sidebar does |

The DAG's own entries and items carry over.
Its menus offer core's board actions, such as Add block, Create link and Remove block, and the DAG's own, Copy, Cut, Paste and Layout.
Its toolbar holds its own controls, search, zoom in, zoom out and fit, and a short list of board actions.
On the board, the list holds Add block, Create link, Create stack, Paste and Layout.
On a selection, it holds Create stack, Add to stack, Copy, Cut and Remove.
A board action that another package adds on the board or on a selection shows in the DAG's menus, but not on its toolbar.
The user opens the menu of the board with a right click on the DAG's canvas, and the menu of a selection with a right click on the selection.

## The status of a block

In blockr.dag, the DAG's method of the generic `extension_block_callback()` of blockr.dock draws a badge on the node of each block that has an error.
In blockr.graph, each node shows the status dot of its block, from the block's status and its notifications, as the dock's card does.
So nothing takes the place of the method.
A script that defines a method of `extension_block_callback()` for the class `dag_extension` drops it.

## Options

The package blockr.dag reads the R option `blockr.dag.svg_renderer`, and g6R, which draws its canvas, reads options of its own.
The package blockr.graph draws with neither G6 nor g6R, and reads none of these options.
So a script drops them:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# blockr.dag
options(
  g6R.mode = "dev",
  g6R.directed_graph = TRUE,
  g6R.layout_on_data_change = TRUE
)

serve(new_dock_board(extensions = new_dag_extension()))
```

```{r}
# blockr.graph
serve(new_board(plugins = list(new_graph_plugin())))
```

What each option did has this place in blockr.graph:

| Option | In blockr.graph |
|---|---|
| `blockr.dag.svg_renderer` | Nothing, since the DAG draws its nodes as elements of the page, rather than on a canvas element |
| `g6R.mode` | Nothing, since the DAG always shows why the board refuses an edit, such as a link that the user drops |
| `g6R.directed_graph` | Nothing, since the DAG reads the links from the board |
| `g6R.layout_on_data_change` | Nothing, since the DAG lays the whole board out again only when someone asks for it ([The layout](#the-layout)) |
| `g6R.preserve_elements_position` | Nothing, since the DAG keeps every position in its state, and draws each block where its state puts it |

## The functions that go

The table gives each function of blockr.dag that is gone, with what takes its place.

| Function of blockr.dag | In blockr.graph |
|---|---|
| `new_dag_extension()` | `new_graph_plugin()`, in the `plugins` of `new_board()` |
| `dag_layout()` | `graph_layout()` |
| `is_dag_layout()` | Nothing, since a script tests `inherits(x, "graph_layout")` |
| `context_menu_items()`, `new_context_menu_entry()` and `is_context_menu_entry()` | A board action, which a plugin class of a package lists ([Menus and the toolbar](#menus-and-the-toolbar)) |
| `toolbar_items()`, `new_toolbar_item()` and `is_toolbar_item()` | A board action, which a plugin class of a package lists ([Menus and the toolbar](#menus-and-the-toolbar)) |
| The DAG's method of `extension_block_callback()` | Nothing, since each node shows the status dot of its block |

The functions of blockr.graph that a script calls are `new_graph_plugin()` and `graph_layout()`.
